entities.name: Klosterneuburg Monastery
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Klosterneuburg Monastery (Stift Klosterneuburg), founded in 1114 CE by Margrave Leopold III of Austria (later canonized) in Lower Austria above the Danube just north of Vienna, is one of Austria's most important and oldest monasteries — housing the Verduner Altar (1181 CE, one of the greatest Romanesque enamel works in Europe, with 51 gilded enamel panels by Nicholas of Verdun), the coronation relics of the Babenberg dynasty, and a remarkable 18th-century imperial residential palace that Charles VI planned to rival Versailles. The monastery is both an active Augustinian canon community and one of Austria's top ten tourist destinations.

Leopold III's founding legend: according to tradition, his wife's veil was blown from Klosterneuburg hill by wind on their wedding night; nine years later, Leopold found it preserved — undamaged — in a briar bush on the exact spot, interpreting this as a divine sign to found a monastery. The Verduner Altar (Klosterneuburger Altar, 1181 CE) — commissioned by Leopold's successor Provost Wernher and created by Nicholas of Verdun — is considered the most important Romanesque enamel work in the world, its 51 panels depicting Old and New Testament typological parallels in translucent enamel on gilded copper.

The 18th-century Habsburg expansion: Emperor Charles VI (r. 1711-1740) planned to transform Klosterneuburg into a Habsburg Escorial — an Austrian equivalent of Philip II's Spanish palace-monastery complex. Only one of nine planned domed towers was completed before Charles's death, but the single baroque dome — topped with an imperial crown and the Habsburg ducal crown (the crown's distinctive arched band) — became the iconic view of Klosterneuburg from the Danube. The monastery winery (one of Austria's largest, with 80 hectares of vineyard) produces award-winning wines.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Klosterneuburg Monastery — housing the greatest Romanesque enamel work in Europe (Verduner Altar) and Austria's founding dynastic relics — is the physical repository of Austria's Babenberg heritage and the site where Habsburg imperial ambition (Charles VI's incomplete Escorial) meets Romanesque artistic achievement.
